To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have performed the first time-resolved serial femtosecond x-ray diffraction experiment and have determined the high-resolution structures of intermediates of the photocycle of a bacterial blue-light photoreceptor, photoactive yellow protein, using x-ray free electron-laser radiation.

we have performed the first femtosecond time-resolved crystal structure determination using an XFEL and that the results reveal structural changes of a light-sensitive protein at 10 ns and at 1 µs following photoexcitation.

time-resolved serial femtosecond protein crystallography is capable of resolving the structural dynamics of a photoactive protein at the level of individual atoms, and that the structural dynamics of the photoactive yellow protein can be resolved at the atomic level in a time-resolved manner.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structural dynamics of photoactive protein systems.

the study of biological processes by time-resolved serial femtosecond x-ray crystallographing (SFXC) using the x-ray free-electron laser (XFEL) at the Linac Coherent Light Source (LCLS) in Stanford, CA.
the development and implementation of new methods for the time-resolved study of the structural dynamics of biomolecules in solution.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results obtained by Tenboer et. al. are a major step forward in the field of time resolved serial crystallographey.
XFELs provide a new method to investigate the structure of biological systems in their native environment.
XFEL serial femtosecond X-ray crystallographic analysis is a powerful method to capture high-resolution intermediates during the light-triggered structural changes of a protein.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we were able to obtain high resolution structures of intermediates of a photobiological reaction.
we used a new technique to study a protein reaction in a way that has never been done before.
we have demonstrated a new technique that can be applied to a broad range of biological systems and that can be used to study a broad range of time scales and structural changes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can now study reversible biological reactions with time resolutions of femtoseconds, which is the fastest time scale accessible by x-ray free electron las-ers.
we have shown that we can do time-resolved crystallo-graphy with a time resolution on the femtosecond timescale and with a resolution of about 1.5 angstroms.
time-resolved serial femtosecond protein crystallography (TR-SFX) can capture the high-resolution structural changes that occur in the course of a biological reaction.
